question.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=4-4z$ at the point $(0,2,2).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =4-4z \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z & =4\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=4.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,2,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,2,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)k \\  & =2x\,i-2y\,j+4\,k \\ ∇f(0,2,2) & =2(0)\,i-2(2)\text{ }j+4\,k \\  & =-4\,j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,-4,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(0,2,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,2,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,2,2⟩+t\,∇f(0,2,2)=⟨0,2,2⟩+t\,⟨0,-4,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$
